4. In reply to the argument advanced by appellant’s Counsel, the learned Deputy Attorney-General argued that if the offences in respect of which the charge-sheet has been submitted against the appellants come under the definition of the term "prejudicial act" then the offences would be offences under the Public Safety Ordinance, 1958 since repealed by the Act and there will be no bar to the prosecution of the appellants as provided under section 36 of the Act. He further argued that the trial involves both substantive and procedural law and that the procedural law must be deemed to have retrospective effect. 

 5. The question involved in this appeal is clearly a question of jurisdiction as to whether the police could submit a charge sheet under section 16(3) of the Act and whether the Special Tribunal constituted under the said Act had jurisdiction to take cognizance of the alleged offences and whether the Tribunal is the proper forum for holding the trial in respect of the said offences when the Act came into force on 9-2-1974 whereas those offences were allegedly committed on 5-2-1974. It is to be noted that there is no dispute that the Act was not given a retrospective effect. So when there was no existence of the Act at the time the alleged offences were committed it passes one's comprehension as to how those offences can be said to be offences under a non-existing enactment and can be tried thereunder. It was, however, urged that if the offences come under the definition of the terns "prejudicial act" within the meaning of section 2(f) (viii) of the Act, then those offences will be offences under the Public Safety Ordinance, 1958 which also made the prejudicial act an offence triable and punishable under the said Ordinance. 

 6. Under section 2(f) (viii) of the Act the term 'prejudicial act' means any act which is intended or likely to prejudice the economic or financial interests of the State. It cannot possibly be denied that counterfeiting Government stamps will surely prejudice the economic or financial interests of the State. But it is to be seen whether the definition of the "prejudicial act" in the Public Safety Ordinance, 1958 corresponds to the definition of the said term in the Act; if so, then the argument that the alleged offences will be offences under the Public Safety Ordinance and that there will be no bar to the prosecution of the appellants under the Act as contemplated under section 36 of the Act will have force. The relevant part of section 36 of the Act reads as under: 

 36. Repeals and Savings.- (1) The Security Act, 1952, (XXXV of 1952) the Public Safety Ordinance 1958 (E.P. Old. LXXVIII of 1958) and the Bangladesh Scheduled Offences (Special Tribunal) Order, 1972 (P.O. 50 of 1972), are hereby repealed. 

 (a) any order or rule made or anything done or any action taken or any proceeding commenced under any provision of the Security Act. 1952 (XXXV of 1952) or the Public Safety Ordinance, 1958 (E.P. Ord. LXXVIII of 1958), shall in so far as it is not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act be deemed to have been made, done, taken or commenced under the corresponding provisions of this act. 

 8. It is obvious that notwithstanding the repeal of the Public Safety Ordinance, 1958 by the Act, any action taken or any proceeding commenced under any provisions of the Public Safety Ordinance, 1958 shall be deemed to have been taken or commenced under the corresponding provisions of the Act, in so far as it is not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act But none of the provisions of section 2(4) of the Public Safety Ordinance since repealed by the Act corresponds to the provision under section 2(f)(viii) of the Act. So the term "prejudicial act" as defined or enumerated under section 2(4) of the Public Safety Ordinance does not cover the definition of the term “prejudicial act” under section 2(f) (viii) of the Act. So section 36 of the Act is not at all attracted as the offences said to have been committed by the appellants did not fall within the ambit of the repealed Public Safety Ordinance. 

 10. Further, section 255 provides that whoever counterfeits or knowingly performs any part of the process of counterfeiting any stamps issued by the Government for the purpose of revenue shall be punished with transportation for life or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to 10 years and shall also be liable to fine while section 256,258 and 259 provide for punishment of either description which may extend to 7 years and also fine. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan pointed out that having invoked section 16(3) of the Act in the charge-sheet and thereby making the case triable by a Special Tribunal there has been a violation of sub Article (1) of Article 35 of the Constitution, which runs as follows: 

 12. In this connection the case of Colonial Sugar Refining Company Ltd. Vs. Irving (1905) Appeal Cases 369, was also referred to. In that case a question as to the extent of retrospectivity to be given to an amending Act was considered. Though in the present case there is no question of retrospectivity of any Act, still we think that certain observation made in that case by their Lordships of the Privy Council will render support to our decision. The facts of that case were that the appellants had disputed the rights of the Collector of Customs for Queensland to levy an excise duty, in respect of 6700 tons of sugar. They brought an action against the Collector to recover the sum they had deposited with him under protest. The writ in the action was issued on October 26, 1902. The Supreme Court of the State decided on September 4, 1903 that the Government was entitled to retain the duty and gave judgment for the Collector with costs. In the meantime the Judiciary Act, 1903, had been passed. It received the Royal assent on August 25, 1903. By section 39 of that Act, it was provided that every decision of a court of a State from which, at the establishment of the Commonwealth, an appeal lay to the Queen in Council, shall be final and conclusive except so far as an appeal may be brought to the High Court of Australia. The appellants, being dissatisfied with the judgment of the Supreme Court of their State, applied to the Court for leave to appeal to His Majesty in Council. The learned Chief Justice thought that leave ought to be granted but the other Judge differed. In accordance with the Order in Council of June 30, 1960, the opinion of the Chief Justice prevailed and leave to appeal was granted. The Commonwealth Collector of Customs for Queensland then challenged the competency of the grant of leave, before the Privy Council. It was observed by their Lordships of the Judicial Committee that if the amendment concerned more than a matter of procedure, if it touched a right in existence at the passing of the Act, in accordance with a long line of authorities, the appellants would be entitled to succeed. The Judiciary Act, it was observed, was not retrospective by express enactment or by necessary intendment. It was found that the right vested in the appellants at the date of the passing of the Act to appeal to His Majesty in Council and to deprive a suit or in a pending action, of an appeal to a superior tribunal, which belonged to him as of right, was a very different thing from regulating the procedure. In principle, their Lordships saw no difference between abolishing an appeal altogether and transferring the appeal to a new tribunal. In either case, it was held, there was interference with existing rights, contrary to the well-known general principle that statutes were not to, be held retrospective unless a clear intention to that effect is manifested.
